questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the binary-search-tree property?

options.text: For every node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all in the right subtree are larger
Every node has at most two children
The left child is smaller than the right child, with no constraint on subtrees
Every level of the tree is completely full

questions.explanation: The property is recursive: the ENTIRE left subtree is smaller than a node and the entire right subtree is larger — not just the immediate children.

questions.prompt: Which traversal of a BST produces keys in ascending sorted order?
questions.explanation: Visiting the smaller left subtree before the node and the larger right subtree after yields ascending order.

questions.prompt: Which statements about BSTs are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Search, insert, and delete are all O(h) where h is the height
In-order traversal lists the keys in sorted order
Inserting sorted keys can degrade a plain BST to O(n) per operation
A plain BST always guarantees O(log n) operations

questions.explanation: Costs are O(h); in-order is sorted; sorted inserts create a degenerate O(n) chain. Only a BALANCED tree guarantees O(log n).

questions.prompt: An ______ traversal of a BST visits keys in ascending sorted order. (one word)
questions.explanation: In-order traversal (left, node, right) exploits the ordering property to emit keys in sorted sequence.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of searching for a key in a BST.

items.text: Compare the key with the current node
Go left if smaller, right if larger
Repeat until found or you reach an empty spot

questions.explanation: BST search follows one root-to-leaf path guided by comparisons, which is why it costs O(h).

questions.prompt: Match each item with its complexity or meaning.

pairs.right: Smallest key in the right subtree

questions.explanation: Balance determines whether search is logarithmic or linear; in-order lists everything sorted; the successor is used in two-child deletion.
